title: Internal search on a documentation site
metaTitle: Search that works inside the docs
excerpt: When the docs are large, search is a primary path. Show the heading that matched, not only the page title. A failed search should offer a way to ask a person.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror, a room full of options for an article about finding the right page in the docs.
caption: Racks you can scan, and a mirror if you need another look. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When do docs need search?
faqs.answer: Add search when a new reader cannot see the right job by scanning the navigation. A short set of task pages can live without a box, while a long reference cannot. Search helps after the jobs are named, and it does not repair a sidebar that is only a list of nouns.

faqs.question: What should a search result show?
faqs.answer: Show the heading that matched, the page it lives on, and a line of the sentence around the match. A list of page titles alone hides the answer inside a long document. Highlight the words they typed, and make the result a link that opens on that heading.

faqs.question: What should happen when nothing matches?
faqs.answer: Say that nothing matched, repeat the query, and offer a next step: a contact path, the main jobs, or the product word you actually use. An empty illustration with no action is a dead end. Do not invent results that do not contain their words.

markdown:
Docs search ux becomes a primary path once the documentation is too long to scan. People arrive with a job and a word. Show them the heading that matched, not only the title of a long page. If nothing matches, give them a way to ask a person.

A dead end in search is a dead end in the product. The box is not a substitute for a table of contents made of jobs. It is how someone reaches the right heading after that structure exists.

## Put the field where the task starts

Place search at the start of the docs, visible without a hunt, with a real label. "Search docs" is a label. A magnifying glass with no name is a guess. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the reference for controls people can perceive and operate: a name, keyboard access, and a visible focus. The field should work if someone never uses a pointer. Placeholder text that disappears is not the label. Keep the label in place.

Many readers will not browse. They have an error string, a field name, or a half-remembered feature. Do not make them open a menu of sixty nouns before they are allowed to type. A keyboard shortcut is a courtesy for people who live in the docs. It is not a replacement for a visible field.

Say what the box covers. Docs, the whole site, or the product. Mixing marketing pages, blog posts, and reference in one unlabeled search produces results that feel random. If you search everything, group the results and put the task pages first. A brand essay above the setup step is a miss even when the essay contains the word.

[People-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page serves the reason someone came. A results page has one purpose: the closest true heading. The query, the matches, the next action. A hero on the results page spends the only moment they are willing to scan.

## Show the heading that matched

A page title is often broader than the question. "Billing" may be the page. "What happens when a card is declined" may be the heading they need. If you only show Billing, they open a long document and hunt again. The search failed in the last inch.

Each result should carry the heading as the link, the page title in smaller type so they know the neighborhood, and a line of context where their words are visible. Two lines are a scan. A full paragraph is another page. If several headings on one page match, show the best two and say there are more, rather than stacking five identical titles.

Rank job pages above raw reference when both match, unless the query looks like an error string or a code. An error string should find the error. "Invite a teammate" should find the task, not a changelog line from last year. Prefer the path that teaches the job. You do not need a complicated ranking story to do that. You need page types and a bias toward the task.

Land them on the heading, not at the top of a page that contains the words somewhere below. The anchor should be copyable. People paste docs links into tickets. A result that only works inside a widget, and cannot be shared, traps the answer in your tab.

## When nothing matches

Say what happened, in text. Repeat the query so a typo is visible. Offer three moves: try a word the product uses, browse the main jobs, or contact a person. An illustration with no sentence is a shrug. Shrugs do not belong in help.

If they typed a synonym and you know the product word, say so. "We call this an invite," and link to that page. Do not silently rewrite their query into a different concept and pretend those were hits. A surprised result is worse than an honest miss, because they stop trusting the box on the next question.

Attach the query to the contact path when you can do it cleanly. The human sees what the docs lacked, and the reader does not retype. Those messages are a writing backlog. A repeated empty query is a missing page or a missing synonym. Read them monthly. Ignoring the list means you will keep losing people who were one word away.

Do not fill the empty state with popular articles that ignore what they typed. Popular is often the getting-started page they have already seen. If you show other pages, label them as suggestions, not as matches. The label is what keeps the habit alive.

## Keyboard, speed, and ugly queries

Results should arrive while typing still feels connected to the list. A spinner that outlasts patience sends people to an outside search engine, which does not know your nouns. Index the docs you actually ship. A stale index sends them to a button you renamed, which is a defect, not a quirk.

Support the keyboard through the whole path. Into the field, down the results, onto the page, and back. Focus has to be visible. A custom list that traps focus is broken for anyone without a pointer, and it is clumsy for everyone else. Test leaving the widget. Pretty is optional. Escape is not.

Plan for queries that look messy and are serious. Pasted error text. A field name. A short code. Accept them without a lecture, and include the error catalog in the index if you have one. If you ignore some punctuation, still find the code. The person who pasted a stack line is already having a bad minute. The box should not add a second one.

Log what you are allowed to log, and review it. You will learn the words customers use. Either adopt their word in the interface or teach the mapping in the empty state and on the page. A search box without that review slowly becomes confident and wrong. Confidence is not the same as a hit.

## What the box should not be asked to do

Search should not be the only map. A reader who does not know the word yet cannot search for it. Browse and search are both doors. Removing the job list because the box exists punishes the person who is new. The jobs stay visible. Search covers the long tail and the exact string.

If every session starts in the box, the navigation is failing. Fix the names of the pages. Use search for the rest. A product that hides fifty tasks behind one field has not organized the docs. It has deferred the decision, and the deferral shows up as repeated queries for the same basic job.

Keep docs search distinct from marketing search if they behave differently. Label the scope. A narrow box is a feature when the label is honest. People should not think the widget forgot the pricing page. The pricing page has its own name and its own place. It does not need to win a query about an error code.

Do not follow people around the web to "improve" this. The improvement is in headings and synonyms. Be plain about what you store on your own site. A help experience that feels like surveillance gets used less, and then the docs get worse. Measure whether they opened a heading, and whether they came back with the same query because it failed.

## Ship the index with the rename

The index is part of the product. When a button changes name, the docs and the search index move in the same release. A result that teaches the old verb is a broken link. Put it on the checklist beside the changelog. The changelog can announce the change. Search has to find the new word on the day it ships.

Give someone the queries. Monthly is enough until the volume is large. The output is a short list: titles to fix, synonyms to add, tasks you have not written. Without an owner, the box lies politely. Owners are how it stays a path.

Test with three real questions from support, on a phone. If a person who knows the product cannot land on the heading, a new customer will not. Fix the result before you restyle the dropdown. The dropdown is not the product. The heading is.

Leadly and Trade Moai, as public interfaces, are built to be scanned. A results list deserves the same scan: the match first, one hierarchy, no pile of equal badges. Use the docs type, not a new face invented for the widget. Search should feel like the documentation, because it is the documentation in a different order.

On a Hanabi docs site this lives in the same Next.js and React system as the rest of the product, with a field that is a real input and results that are real links. Tailwind keeps the list in the reading styles. The client should be able to see where the strings live in the repository they own, so a rename is a change they can follow, not a mystery inside a vendor widget.

## The limit of a better box

A careful search will not explain a concept you never wrote. It will not carry an outage. It will not replace a person for the weird case. Write the jobs, title them as jobs, then let search reach the headings. If you start with the box, you will index a warehouse and call it help.

When the next step is a form, the same care about labels and errors applies. [Forms that do not feel like paperwork](/blog/forms-that-do-not-feel-like-paperwork) is that piece. Read it if an empty search dumps people into a contact form that asks twelve questions before it accepts the one they already typed.

If you want the docs, the titles, and the search to behave as one path, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring a query your users actually type. The right result is a heading, not a tour of the system.
